title: Maru, looking back
hook: the raga of courage holds some of the Granth's longest hymns
tomorrow: what if every month of the year were a love letter?

segments.voice: Yesterday, who but you: Ravidas under a royal canopy, read as dignity here and as honor before God. That was Maru's last hymn. Today we look back at the whole raga.

Courage shows up in the hands first. Sweaty palms before a talk. A tight grip on the wheel on a first drive. A hand that won't let go of someone else's. Simran saw it this week in the smallest way. Fateh, her little cousin, tied his own patka for the first time, alone in front of the mirror. It came out crooked. When she reached to fix it, he pulled away: no, mine. That's what courage feels like in your hands. Maru, looked at one more time, is full of hands.

Maru runs from ang 989 to ang 1106, and tradition links it with courage and the field of battle. It holds long hymns, the Solhe, and ballads, and the Bhagats at the end. Hold it up and look at the hands. First, a coin in the palm: Guru Nanak's test, where real silver rings true whatever's scrawled on the paper. Then cupped hands, the Anjulian, and the riddle of plenty and little. Hands over the eyes in the dark before creation, which turned out to be full. A face turned toward the Guru, and a humble traveler's open hands, answering mockery with peace. Bebe's floury hand, pressing one couplet into Simran's: when You are on my side. Kabir's warrior, who doesn't leave the field. And Ravidas, lifted under a canopy he didn't build. Put together, Maru's courage is almost never a fist. It's a hand that trusts, receives, holds on, and refuses to let go of what's right. Brave in faith.

segments.voice: Choose your favorite Maru line from these days and say it once, slowly, while pressing your palms firmly together. Then let your hands fall open in your lap, palms up. Stay there, open but steady, for the rest of the sit.
Maru: the raga tradition ties to courage, from ang 989 to 1106, now walked from end to end.
For the road: brave in faith, an open hand that still holds on. Fifteen-seventy-nine, palms open.

howItsDone: Hymns in raga Maru are sung in kirtan at the gurdwara and read in order during a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; Kabir's true-warrior salok and Ravidas's 'who but You' are often heard among them.

chat.says: fateh tied his own patka today. so crooked. wouldn't let me fix it lol. should i have?
options: No. His hands, his crooked courage. Brave in faith grows when he does it himself.
Yes. A patka has to look perfect, or the brave part doesn't really count.
Yes. Courage in Maru means never letting anyone see you get it wrong.
chat.meaning: Maru's courage is a hand that trusts and holds on, not a perfect result. Fateh's crooked patka is his own brave hand.
